Business Activity: Company Identity

Launching Your Creationeering™ Vehicle Company

Lesson Overview

Every great product starts with more than just a good idea — it starts with a team that knows who they are and where they're going. In this activity, you'll establish a formal business identity for your mousetrap vehicle company. That means naming your company, writing a mission statement, assigning leadership roles, mapping out your organizational structure, and setting clear goals. These aren't just paperwork exercises. They're the same foundational steps real engineering firms take before a single bolt is tightened or a dollar is spent.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this activity, you will be able to:

  • Write a mission statement that reflects both engineering excellence and ethical stewardship.
  • Assign and explain the responsibilities of five key leadership roles in an engineering company.
  • Create an organizational chart showing how information flows through your team.
  • Build a production timeline using a Gantt chart and identify the critical path.
  • Define measurable success metrics for your company's launch.
  • Connect business planning to the biblical principle of faithful stewardship.

items.definition: A short, clear declaration of a company's purpose, values, and commitment to the people it serves.
A diagram that shows the structure of a team or company — who leads, who reports to whom, and how information flows.
A visual timeline that maps out tasks, their durations, and when each must be completed during a project.
The sequence of tasks that absolutely must stay on schedule — if any one of them is delayed, the whole project is delayed.
Anyone who is affected by or has an interest in the outcome of your project — customers, teammates, and community included.
Specific, measurable goals that tell you whether your project has achieved what you set out to do.

data.html:
Part 1: Company Identity and Mission

Before an engineering team designs a single component, the best ones ask a deeper question: Why are we doing this? Your company needs a "North Star" — a guiding purpose that shapes every decision from the drawing board to the finish line. That's exactly what a mission statement provides.

A strong mission statement does two things at once. It tells the world what you build, and it tells the world how and why you build it. Notice how that goes beyond just making a fast car. It reflects your obligation to your customers (quality and safety), your teammates (respect and trust), and your broader community (service and stewardship).

Proverbs 29:18 — "Where there is no vision, the people perish." A mission statement isn't just a business tool — it's a vision. It keeps your team unified and your work purposeful. God gave His people the Law, the Prophets, and ultimately His Son to make His mission clear. Your company deserves the same kind of clarity.

Write Your Company Name and Mission Statement

Start by giving your company a name that reflects who you are as a team. Then craft a 2–3 sentence mission statement. Here's an example to get you thinking:

"To provide innovative, high-performance kinetic transport solutions while honoring our resources through sustainable design and ethical craftsmanship."

Notice what that example does well: it names the product (kinetic transport solutions), describes the quality standard (high-performance), and ties it to values (sustainable design, ethical craftsmanship). Yours should do the same — in your own words.

  • Company Name: ________________________________________________
  • Mission Statement: ________________________________________________

Writing tip: A great mission statement avoids vague words like "good" or "the best." Instead, be specific. What does your vehicle do? Who does it serve? What values guide how you build it? Answering those three questions will get you 90% of the way there.

Part 2: Leadership Roles

A company without clear roles is like a vehicle with no steering — everyone's pushing energy somewhere, but nobody's sure where it's going. Assign one team member to each of the five key positions below. Each role corresponds to a critical "pillar" of the Engineering Lifecycle, from technical design all the way to legal compliance.

This isn't just an assignment of names to job titles. It's a commitment. The person who takes on a role is responsible for that area — they make calls, they track progress, and they answer for outcomes. That's accountability, and it's one of the most important habits any engineer — or any leader — can develop.

The Five Pillars of Your Team

  • CEO (Chief Executive Officer): Oversees the entire project, ensures deadlines are met, and leads team meetings. This person keeps everyone rowing in the same direction. Team Member: ________________
  • Chief Engineer: Manages the design, testing, and technical integrity of the vehicle. If there's a build decision to make, it goes through this person. Team Member: ________________
  • Head of Sales: Responsible for marketing the vehicle and communicating its value to customers. This role is all about telling your story compellingly. Team Member: ________________
  • Finance Manager: Tracks the budget, manages resource costs, and ensures financial stewardship. Every dollar in your materials list is their responsibility. Team Member: ________________
  • Legal Officer: Ensures compliance with project rules, safety standards, and ethical guidelines. This person is the conscience of the operation. Team Member: ________________

Real-world connection: In professional engineering firms, these roles exist in every department — sometimes held by one person, sometimes by entire teams. The Legal Officer role, for example, mirrors what real companies call a "compliance officer" — someone whose entire job is making sure the team never cuts ethical corners, even under deadline pressure.

Part 3: Management Structure and Execution

Knowing who is on your team is just the start. Now you need to know how your team works together and when things need to happen. This section covers two powerful planning tools that professional engineers use on every major project: organizational charts and Gantt charts.

Organizational Chart

An organizational chart — or "org chart" — is a visual map of your team's hierarchy. Think of it like a flowchart for people. It shows who leads, who reports to whom, and how decisions and information move through the group.

Draw your org chart in the space below. Start with your CEO at the top. Then show how the other four roles connect. Ask yourself: does the Head of Sales report to the CEO directly? Does the Chief Engineer consult with the Finance Manager before ordering materials? Those relationships matter — map them out.

data.caption: Example organizational chart showing CEO at the top with four department leads branching below, including arrows showing communication flow between roles.

data.html:
The Production Gantt Chart and Critical Path

A Gantt chart is a timeline on a grid. Each row is a task; each column is a unit of time (days, class periods, weeks). You shade in the blocks where that task is active. At a glance, you — and anyone on your team — can see exactly what's happening and when.

Here are the major milestones to map out for your mousetrap vehicle project:

  • Design — Sketching, measuring, planning materials
  • Prototype — Building the first version
  • Testing — Running trials, recording data, identifying failures
  • Final Build — Making improvements and completing the final vehicle
  • Marketing — Preparing your pitch and presentation

Once your chart is drawn, identify the Critical Path: which tasks absolutely cannot be delayed without pushing back your entire launch date? Circle or highlight those on your chart. That's where your team needs to protect its time most fiercely.

data.caption: Sample Gantt chart template with rows for each project milestone and columns for each class period or week, with the critical path highlighted.

data.html: Luke 14:28 — "Suppose one of you wants to build a tower. Won't you first sit down and estimate the cost to see if you have enough money to complete it?" Jesus used a construction analogy to teach about counting the cost before committing. Your Gantt chart is exactly that — sitting down, estimating what it will take, and making sure you can finish what you start.

The Three Ts of Stewardship: As you plan your production timeline, think carefully about how your team will manage its three most important resources — Time (your schedule), Talent (your roles and strengths), and Treasury (your materials and budget). A team that manages all three well rarely runs out of any of them.

Part 4: Success Metrics

Here's a question every engineer eventually has to answer: How do you know when you're done? More importantly — how do you know when you've succeeded? Vague goals like "do well" or "build a good car" don't cut it in engineering. You need measurable targets you can actually check off.

Define three specific success metrics for your company's launch. A good metric has a number or a clear condition attached to it. Instead of "our vehicle should go far," try "our vehicle will travel at least 5 meters on a single mousetrap release." Instead of "we want to stay on budget," try "we will complete the final build spending no more than $8.00 in materials."

Write your three success metrics below:

  • Metric 1: ________________________________________________
  • Metric 2: ________________________________________________
  • Metric 3: ________________________________________________

Watch out for fuzzy goals. "Build a vehicle that works" is not a success metric — it's a hope. Real metrics are specific and testable. If you can't answer "yes" or "no" to whether you hit the goal, rewrite it until you can. Vague goals lead to vague results.

Bringing It All Together

What you've built in this activity isn't just a class assignment — it's the actual foundation of how real companies launch real products. A mission that guides your decisions. Roles that distribute responsibility. A timeline that keeps the work on track. And metrics that tell you, without guessing, whether you succeeded.

Engineering is never just about the thing you build. It's about the team you build it with, the integrity you bring to the process, and the people you're ultimately building it for. That's Creationeering. Now go build something worth launching.

data.html:
1. What is the purpose of a mission statement, and what two obligations should it reflect?

2. Which leadership role is responsible for ensuring the team follows safety standards and ethical guidelines?

3. What is the difference between a Gantt chart and an organizational chart? What does each one show?

4. In your own words, explain what the "critical path" means. Why does it matter for your project timeline?

5. Why is it important for success metrics to be specific and measurable rather than general and vague?
